claims.claim: EphrinB2 upregulation was localized to GFAP-expressing astrocytes in the ventral horn at disease endstage.
claims.source: EphrinB2 upregulation was localized to GFAP-expressing astrocytes (Figure 1o–q) and was not co-localized to NeuN-expressing neurons (Figure 1l–n; n=3 mice).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by double immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1o-q demonstrating co-localization of ephrinB2 with GFAP.

claims.claim: EphrinB2 was not co-localized to NeuN-expressing neurons in the ventral horn at disease endstage.
claims.source: EphrinB2 upregulation was localized to GFAP-expressing astrocytes (Figure 1o–q) and was not co-localized to NeuN-expressing neurons (Figure 1l–n; n=3 mice).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by double immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1l-n demonstrating lack of co-localization of ephrinB2 with NeuN.

claims.claim: The majority of GFP-expressing cells in ventral horn following lentiviral injection were GFAP+ reactive astrocytes.
claims.source: The majority of GFP-expressing cells in ventral horn were GFAP+ reactive astrocytes; these GFAP+/GFP+ astrocytes also expressed high levels of ephrinB2, demonstrating that the lentiviral constructs targeted reactive astrocytes that included those with upregulated ephrinB2 expression (Figure 2j–l).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2j-l and quantified in Figure 2m showing 56.53±5.30% of GFP+ cells were GFAP+.

claims.claim: There was little-to-no co-labeling of the GFP reporter with NeuN+ neurons following lentiviral injection.
claims.source: On the contrary, there was little-to-no co-labeling of the GFP reporter with NeuN+ neurons (Figure 2d–f) or cells positive for oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2 (Olig2) (Figure 2g–i), demonstrating that the injected viral constructs did not target a large portion of neurons or cells of the oligodendrocyte lineage within the ventral horn.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2d-f and quantified in Figure 2m showing only 3.54±1.09% of GFP+ cells were NeuN+.

claims.claim: There was little-to-no co-labeling of the GFP reporter with Olig2+ cells following lentiviral injection.
claims.source: On the contrary, there was little-to-no co-labeling of the GFP reporter with NeuN+ neurons (Figure 2d–f) or cells positive for oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2 (Olig2) (Figure 2g–i), demonstrating that the injected viral constructs did not target a large portion of neurons or cells of the oligodendrocyte lineage within the ventral horn.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2g-i and quantified in Figure 2m showing only 0.18±0.18% of GFP+ cells were Olig2+.

claims.claim: The lenti-shRNA vector reduced ephrinB2 expression by approximately a factor of 5 compared to lenti-GFP control.
claims.source: Compared to lenti-GFP control (Figure 2o–q), the lenti-shRNA (Figure 2p–r) reduced ephrinB2 expression by approximately a factor of 5 (Lenti-GFP: 86.92±22.35 GFP+/ephrinB2+ cells, n=3 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 16.67±1.76 GFP+/ephrinB2+ cells, n=3 mice mice; t-test, p=0.035; Figure 2n).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of ephrinB2+/GFP+ cells shown in Figure 2n-r.

claims.claim: Following transduction of Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2, there was a significantly greater number of motor neurons within the ventral horn compared to Lenti-GFP controls in C3-C5 spinal cord.
claims.source: In C3, C4, and C5 following transduction of Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 (Figure 3d), there was a significantly greater number of MNs within the ventral horn compared to Lenti-GFP controls (Figure 3c) (Lenti-GFP: 266.4±19.46 MNs/µm2, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2: 344.3±6.31 MNs/µm2, n=4 mice; p=0.019, t-test) (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motor neuron counts from cresyl violet stained sections shown in Figure 3a-d and quantified in Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Quantification of CMAP amplitude showed a 61% larger amplitude for the lenti-shRNA group compared to lenti-GFP.
claims.source: Quantification of CMAP amplitude showed a 61% larger amplitude for the lenti-shRNA group (Figure 3f) compared to lenti-GFP (Figure 3e–g), demonstrating that ephrinB2 knockdown in cervical ventral horn resulted in significant preservation of functional diaphragm innervation (Lenti-GFP: 2.58±0.26 mV, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 4.20±0.32 mV, n=4 mice; t-test, p=0.0075).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by CMAP recordings shown in Figure 3e-g.

claims.claim: EphrinB2 knockdown had no impact on overall disease phenotype, including limb motor function, disease onset and progression, and animal survival.
claims.source: As expected, given that injections were delivered only to levels C3-5, ephrinB2 knockdown in astrocytes had no impact on overall disease phenotype, including limb motor function, disease onset and progression, and animal survival, as assessed by a battery of established measurements (Lepore et al., 2008b; Lepore et al., 2011b; Lepore et al., 2010; Lepore et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple behavioral and survival measurements shown in Figure 4, including weight loss, grip strength, disease onset, and survival analyses.

claims.claim: EphrinB2 knockdown did not affect weight loss at any age tested.
claims.source: EphrinB2 knockdown did not affect weight loss at any age tested (F (1, 18)=0.17, p=0.69) (Figure 4a; n=8–10 mice per group).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by weight measurements shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: Overall disease onset as determined by the timing of weight loss onset was unaffected by ephrinB2 knockdown.
claims.source: Additionally, overall disease onset as determined by the timing of weight loss onset was unaffected, with both the lenti-GFP and lenti-shRNA groups showing similar onset as determined by Kaplan-Meier analysis (Lenti-GFP: 124.4 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 123.5 days, chi square: 0.017, p=0.90, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=8–9 mice per group) (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis of weight loss onset shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: There were no differences between the two groups in either hindlimb or forelimb grip strength decline.
claims.source: Furthermore, there were no differences between the two groups in either hindlimb (F (1, 18)=0.48, p=0.50, ANOVA; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4c) or forelimb (F (1, 18)=0.95, p=0.34, ANOVA; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4e) grip strength decline.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength measurements shown in Figure 4c and 4e.

claims.claim: EphrinB2 knockdown had no effect on hindlimb disease onset.
claims.source: EphrinB2 knockdown had no effect on either hindlimb disease onset (Lenti-GFP: 90.4 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 103.0 days, chi square: 2.92, p=0.09, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4d) or forelimb disease onset (Lenti-GFP: 107.2 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 105.1 days, chi square: 0.13, p=0.72, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4f).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis of hindlimb disease onset shown in Figure 4d.

claims.claim: EphrinB2 knockdown had no effect on forelimb disease onset.
claims.source: EphrinB2 knockdown had no effect on either hindlimb disease onset (Lenti-GFP: 90.4 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 103.0 days, chi square: 2.92, p=0.09, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4d) or forelimb disease onset (Lenti-GFP: 107.2 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 105.1 days, chi square: 0.13, p=0.72, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=9–10 mice per group) (Figure 4f).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis of forelimb disease onset shown in Figure 4f.

claims.claim: Compared to lenti-GFP control, lenti-shRNA had no effect on disease duration as measured by the time from weight onset to endstage.
claims.source: Compared to lenti-GFP control, lenti-shRNA had no effect on disease duration as measured by the time from: weight onset to endstage (Lenti-GFP: 7.90±1.110 days, n=10 mice; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2: 11.38±1.963 days, p=0.13, unpaired t-test; n=8 mice) (Figure 4g); hindlimb disease onset to endstage (Lenti-GFP: 41.90±6.63 days, n=10 mice; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2: 29.44±6.34 days, n=9 mice, p=0.19, unpaired t-test) (Figure 4h); forelimb disease onset to endstage (Lenti-GFP: 25.10±6.48 days, n=10 mice; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2: 27.11±8.92 days, n=9 mice, p=0.86, unpaired t-test) (Figure 4i); or hindlimb disease onset to forelimb disease onset (Lenti-GFP: 16.80±4.14 days, n=10 mice; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2: 2.33±7.44 days, n=9 mice, p=0.099, unpaired t-test) (Figure 4j).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by disease duration measurements shown in Figure 4g.

claims.claim: Compared to lenti-GFP control, lenti-shRNA had no effect on the age of disease endstage as determined by the righting reflex.
claims.source: Compared to lenti-GFP control, lenti-shRNA had no effect on the age of disease endstage as determined by Kaplan-Meier analysis (Lenti-GFP: 132.3 days; Lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 129.5 days, chi square: 0.24, p=0.63, Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test; n=8–10 mice per group) (Figure 4k).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4k.

claims.claim: The lenti-shRNA group showed a significant increase in the percentage of fully-innervated NMJs compared to control-treated animals.
claims.source: Compared to control-treated animals (Figure 5d), the lenti-shRNA group (Figure 5e) showed a significant increase in the percentage of fully-innervated NMJs (Figure 5f) and a significant decrease in percentage of completely-denervated junctions (Figure 5g), demonstrating that lenti-shRNA treatment preserved PhMN innervation of the diaphragm (innervated: Lenti-GFP: 27.0 ± 2.5% of total NMJs, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 53.2±8.5, n=4; t-test, p=0.04) (denervated: Lenti-GFP: 21.6 ± 1.6% of total NMJs, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 8.0±3.7, n=4 mice; t-test, p=0.03).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by NMJ morphology analysis shown in Figure 5d-f.

claims.claim: The lenti-shRNA group showed a significant decrease in percentage of completely-denervated NMJs compared to control-treated animals.
claims.source: Compared to control-treated animals (Figure 5d), the lenti-shRNA group (Figure 5e) showed a significant increase in the percentage of fully-innervated NMJs (Figure 5f) and a significant decrease in percentage of completely-denervated junctions (Figure 5g), demonstrating that lenti-shRNA treatment preserved PhMN innervation of the diaphragm (innervated: Lenti-GFP: 27.0 ± 2.5% of total NMJs, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 53.2±8.5, n=4; t-test, p=0.04) (denervated: Lenti-GFP: 21.6 ± 1.6% of total NMJs, n=4 mice; Lenti-shRNA: 8.0±3.7, n=4 mice; t-test, p=0.03).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by NMJ morphology analysis shown in Figure 5d-e and 5g.

claims.claim: In the lumbar enlargement, there was a large increase in ephrinB2 protein expression in the SOD1 mutation ALS samples compared to the non-diseased controls.
claims.source: In the lumbar enlargement, there was a large increase in ephrinB2 protein expression in the SOD1 mutation ALS samples compared to the non-diseased controls (Figure 6) (non-ALS lumbar: 3.8±1.1 a.u.; ALS lumbar: 17.8±18.2; ALS cortex: 2.9±0.25; p=0.523, ANOVA).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting analysis on postmortem human samples shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Dramatic ephrinB2 upregulation in the SOD1 mutation samples was observed with only two of the three ALS donors.
claims.source: There was some donor-to-donor variability; while all of the non-ALS control samples showed similarly lower levels of ephrinB2 protein expression in the lumbar spinal cord, dramatic ephrinB2 upregulation in the SOD1 mutation samples was observed with only two of the three ALS donors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6 showing variability across ALS donors.

claims.claim: GFAP protein levels were significantly higher in the two ALS samples with increased ephrinB2 expression.
claims.source: To this point, we also performed GFAP immunoblotting on the same lumbar spinal cord samples and found signficantly higher GFAP protein levels in the two samples with increased ephrinB2 expression (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GFAP immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: EphrinB2 protein levels were not elevated in the frontal cortex of ALS donor samples.
claims.source: Lastly, we did not observe increased ephrinB2 expression in a disease unaffected region in these same three ALS donor samples, as ephrinB2 protein levels were not elevated in frontal cortex (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblotting data from frontal cortex samples shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: EphrinB2 is expressed predominantly by ventral horn astrocytes in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS.
claims.source: We have shown that ephrinB2 is expressed predominantly by ventral horn astrocytes and that ephrinB2 up-regulation coincided with progression of MN loss and overall disease phenotype in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization of ephrinB2 with GFAP and the quantification of transduced cell types.

claims.claim: EphrinB2 up-regulation coincided with progression of motor neuron loss and overall disease phenotype in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS.
claims.source: We have shown that ephrinB2 is expressed predominantly by ventral horn astrocytes and that ephrinB2 up-regulation coincided with progression of MN loss and overall disease phenotype in the SOD1G93A mouse model of ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal analysis of ephrinB2 expression at different disease stages (60 days, 120 days, endstage) shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Reducing ephrinB2 expression in ventral horn astrocytes of the SOD1G93A mouse cervical spinal cord maintained diaphragmatic respiratory function by protecting cervical spinal cord motor neurons.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that reducing ephrinB2 expression in ventral horn astrocytes of the SOD1G93A mouse cervical spinal cord maintained diaphragmatic respiratory function by protecting cervical spinal cord MNs and preserving PhMN innervation of the diaphragm.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the motor neuron counts, CMAP recordings, and NMJ morphology data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claims.claim: Reducing ephrinB2 expression in ventral horn astrocytes of the SOD1G93A mouse cervical spinal cord maintained diaphragmatic respiratory function by preserving phrenic motor neuron innervation of the diaphragm.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that reducing ephrinB2 expression in ventral horn astrocytes of the SOD1G93A mouse cervical spinal cord maintained diaphragmatic respiratory function by protecting cervical spinal cord MNs and preserving PhMN innervation of the diaphragm.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the CMAP recordings and NMJ morphology data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claims.claim: Astrocyte ephrinB2 may play a non-cell autonomous role in ALS, in particular in mutant SOD1-associated disease.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that astrocyte ephrinB2 may play a non-cell autonomous role in ALS, in particular in mutant SOD1-associated disease.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings showing that reducing ephrinB2 in astrocytes protects motor neurons.

claims.claim: Astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis via loss of critically important functions such as extracellular glutamate uptake.
claims.source: A substantial body of work has demonstrated that astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis (Ilieva et al., 2009; Yamanaka and Komine, 2018), both via loss of critically important functions such as extracellular glutamate uptake (Rothstein et al., 1995) and toxic gain-of-function such as altered transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) signaling (Phatnani et al., 2013) and increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Cassina et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on astrocyte dysfunction in ALS.

claims.claim: Astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis via toxic gain-of-function such as altered TGFβ signaling.
claims.source: A substantial body of work has demonstrated that astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis (Ilieva et al., 2009; Yamanaka and Komine, 2018), both via loss of critically important functions such as extracellular glutamate uptake (Rothstein et al., 1995) and toxic gain-of-function such as altered transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) signaling (Phatnani et al., 2013) and increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Cassina et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on TGFβ signaling in ALS astrocytes.

claims.claim: Astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis via toxic gain-of-function such as increased production of reactive oxygen species.
claims.source: A substantial body of work has demonstrated that astrocytes are involved in ALS pathogenesis (Ilieva et al., 2009; Yamanaka and Komine, 2018), both via loss of critically important functions such as extracellular glutamate uptake (Rothstein et al., 1995) and toxic gain-of-function such as altered transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) signaling (Phatnani et al., 2013) and increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Cassina et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on ROS production by astrocytes in ALS.

claims.claim: EphA4 receptor can be activated by ephrinA and ephrinB ligands including ephrinB2.
claims.source: EphA4 receptor can be activated by ephrinA and ephrinB ligands including ephrinB2 (Flanagan and Vanderhaeghen, 1998), suggesting that astocyte ephrinB2 serves as a ligand mediating pathogenic actions in ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA4 receptor-ligand interactions.

claims.claim: Astrocyte ephrinB2 serves as a ligand mediating pathogenic actions in ALS.
claims.source: EphA4 receptor can be activated by ephrinA and ephrinB ligands including ephrinB2 (Flanagan and Vanderhaeghen, 1998), suggesting that astocyte ephrinB2 serves as a ligand mediating pathogenic actions in ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the known receptor-ligand interactions and the experimental findings in the study.

claims.claim: Genetic reduction of EphA4 in SOD1G93A mice did not impact disease measures.
claims.source: Subsequent work in mouse models (Ling et al., 2018; Rué et al., 2019b; Zhao et al., 2018) showed that genetic reduction of EphA4 in SOD1G93A mice or intracerebroventricular delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide directed against EphA4 in both SOD1G93A and PFN1G118V mouse models of ALS did not impact disease measures.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on EphA4 genetic reduction studies in ALS models.

claims.claim: Intracerebroventricular delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide directed against EphA4 in SOD1G93A and PFN1G118V mouse models of ALS did not impact disease measures.
claims.source: Subsequent work in mouse models (Ling et al., 2018; Rué et al., 2019b; Zhao et al., 2018) showed that genetic reduction of EphA4 in SOD1G93A mice or intracerebroventricular delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide directed against EphA4 in both SOD1G93A and PFN1G118V mouse models of ALS did not impact disease measures.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on antisense oligonucleotide studies targeting EphA4 in ALS models.

claims.claim: Administration of an EphA4 agonist to mutant SOD1 mouse increased both disease duration and animal survival.
claims.source: In contrast, manipulations that target EphA4 signaling such as administration of an EphA4 agonist to mutant SOD1 mouse increased both disease duration and animal survival (Wu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA4 agonist treatment in ALS models.

claims.claim: Delivery of soluble EphA4-Fc that blocks ligand binding to EphA4 results in partial preservation of motor function in SOD1G93A mice.
claims.source: In addition, delivery of soluble EphA4-Fc that blocks ligand binding to EphA4 results in partial preservation of motor function in SOD1G93A mice (Zhao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on EphA4-Fc treatment in ALS models.

claims.claim: Genetic knockdown of ephrinA5 in the SOD1G93A mouse model accelerates disease progression and hastens animal death.
claims.source: Supporting this notion, genetic knockdown of ephrinA5 (an EphA4 ligand) in the SOD1G93A mouse model accelerates disease progression and hastens animal death (Rué et al., 2019a), which may be explained by an enhancement of the EphA4-ephrinB2 interaction in the absence of ephrinA5.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on ephrinA5 knockdown in ALS models.

claims.claim: The acceleration of disease progression following ephrinA5 knockdown may be explained by an enhancement of the EphA4-ephrinB2 interaction in the absence of ephrinA5.
claims.source: Supporting this notion, genetic knockdown of ephrinA5 (an EphA4 ligand) in the SOD1G93A mouse model accelerates disease progression and hastens animal death (Rué et al., 2019a), which may be explained by an enhancement of the EphA4-ephrinB2 interaction in the absence of ephrinA5.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the mechanism underlying the ephrinA5 knockdown phenotype.

claims.claim: Directly targeting ephrinB2 is a promising strategy to modulate both Eph-ephrin signaling and astrocyte-motor neuron interactions in ALS.
claims.source: While other agents are also being developed to manipulate binding of ephrins with EphA4 for ALS therapeutics (Qin et al., 2015; Schoonaert et al., 2017), our results suggest that directly targeting ephrinB2 is a promising strategy to modulate both Eph-ephrin signaling and astrocyte-MN interactions in ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing motor neuron protection and functional preservation following ephrinB2 knockdown.

claims.claim: Unlike the effects of knocking down EphA4 expression in ALS animal models, significant motor neuron protection, maintenance of NMJ innervation and preservation of diaphragm muscle function was observed following ephrinB2 reduction.
claims.source: Unlike the effects of knocking down EphA4 expression in ALS animal models, we observe significant MN protection, maintenance of NMJ innervation and preservation of diaphragm muscle function following ephrinB2 reduction.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the study showing these protective effects, in contrast to cited literature on EphA4 knockdown.

claims.claim: Ephrin-B upregulation in chronic pain models results in increased NMDA receptor function and pathological synaptic plasticity via interaction with EphBs.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, ephrin-B upregulation in chronic pain models results in increased NMDA receptor function and pathological synaptic plasticity via interaction with EphBs (Henderson and Dalva, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on ephrin-B signaling in chronic pain.

claims.claim: EphBs are centrally involved in regulating subcellular localization of ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits to excitatory synapses.
claims.source: EphB's are centrally involved in regulating subcellular localization of ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits to excitatory synapses (Hanamura et al., 2017; Nolt et al., 2011), raising the intriguing possibility that enhanced ephrinB2-EphB2 signaling results in increased glutamate receptor activation in MNs and consequently may be contributing to excitotoxicity that plays a well-known role in ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on EphB function in glutamate receptor localization.

claims.claim: Enhanced ephrinB2-EphB2 signaling may result in increased glutamate receptor activation in motor neurons and consequently may be contributing to excitotoxicity in ALS.
claims.source: EphB's are centrally involved in regulating subcellular localization of ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits to excitatory synapses (Hanamura et al., 2017; Nolt et al., 2011), raising the intriguing possibility that enhanced ephrinB2-EphB2 signaling results in increased glutamate receptor activation in MNs and consequently may be contributing to excitotoxicity that plays a well-known role in ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation about a potential mechanism linking ephrinB2 upregulation to excitotoxicity in ALS.

claims.claim: Single-nucleus RNAseq on mouse cervical spinal cord shows that alpha motor neurons of the cervical spinal cord express various EphA and EphB receptors.
claims.source: Consistent with these studies, single-nucleus RNAseq on mouse cervical spinal cord shows that alpha MNs of the cervical spinal cord express various EphA and EphB receptors (http://spinalcordatlas.org/) (Alkaslasi et al., 2021; Blum et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published single-nucleus RNAseq data.

claims.claim: Phrenic motor neurons express a number of EphA and EphB receptors, including EphA4.
claims.source: In addition, this dataset identifies a PhMN-specific marker (ErbB4); by specifically looking at the expression profile of only the ErbB4-expressing cervical alpha MNs, the data reveal that PhMNs express a number of EphA's and EphB's, including EphA4.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of published single-nucleus RNAseq data and IHC validation mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The effect of Efnb2-shRNA treatment was primarily due to changes in astrocytes.
claims.source: However, we observed (1) dramatic ephrinB2 upregulation in the ventral horn of SOD1G93A mice that appears to be astrocyte-specific, (2) transduction predominately of astrocytes with our vector, and (3) significant reduction of ephrinB2 expression almost entirely in astrocytes in shRNA-treated animals. These data suggest that the effect of Efnb2-shRNA treatment was primarily due to changes in astrocytes and that astrocyte expression is the likely mechanism underlying ephrinB2's action in mutant SOD1-associated ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple lines of experimental evidence showing astrocyte-specific ephrinB2 upregulation and knockdown.

claims.claim: Astrocyte expression is the likely mechanism underlying ephrinB2's action in mutant SOD1-associated ALS.
claims.source: However, we observed (1) dramatic ephrinB2 upregulation in the ventral horn of SOD1G93A mice that appears to be astrocyte-specific, (2) transduction predominately of astrocytes with our vector, and (3) significant reduction of ephrinB2 expression almost entirely in astrocytes in shRNA-treated animals. These data suggest that the effect of Efnb2-shRNA treatment was primarily due to changes in astrocytes and that astrocyte expression is the likely mechanism underlying ephrinB2's action in mutant SOD1-associated ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings showing astrocyte-specific effects.

claims.claim: There is a modest increase in astrocyte number in ventral horn of the SOD1G93A mouse model at time points following phenotypic disease onset.
claims.source: We previously showed that there is a modest increase in astrocyte number in ventral horn of the SOD1G93A mouse model at time points following phenotypic disease onset (Lepore et al., 2008a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: The total increase in ephrinB2 expression across the ventral horn was not due to just the small increase in astrocyte numbers but was instead due to the dramatically elevated ephrinB2 expression observed across the astrocyte population.
claims.source: Throughout disease course in these SOD1G93A mice, ephrinB2 level in individual astrocytes dramatically increases (including across most or all astrocytes), suggesting that the total increase in ephrinB2 expression across the ventral horn was not due to just this small increase in astrocyte numbers but was instead due to the dramatically elevated ephrinB2 expression observed across the astrocyte population.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that ephrinB2 levels increase dramatically in individual astrocytes.

claims.claim: ALS is heterogeneous both with respect to its genetic basis and its clinical disease course.
claims.source: ALS is heterogeneous both with respect to its genetic basis and its clinical disease course (e.g. age and site of onset; severity/progression; Mitsumoto et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on ALS heterogeneity and is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Patients with mutations in the same gene show variability in their clinical disease manifestation such as the rate of disease progression depending on the specific SOD1 mutation.
claims.source: Furthermore, these familial cases are associated with mutations in a number of different genes. In addition, patients (even with mutations in the same gene) show variability in their clinical disease manifestation such as the rate of disease progression depending on, for example, the specific SOD1 mutation (Andersen et al., 1997; Radunovíc and Leigh, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on genotype-phenotype correlations in ALS.

claims.claim: Respiratory function involves the contribution of a number of other muscle groups besides diaphragm, and these muscles are innervated by various lower motor neuron pools located across a relatively-large expanse of the CNS neuraxis.
claims.source: Respiratory function involves the contribution of a number of other muscle groups besides diaphragm, and these muscles are innervated by various lower MN pools located across a relatively-large expanse of the CNS neuraxis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of respiratory neuroanatomy.

claims.claim: CMAP recording is a powerful assay of functional innervation of diaphragm muscle by phrenic motor axons.
claims.source: While CMAP recording is a powerful assay of functional innervation of diaphragm muscle by phrenic motor axons, it does not directly measure overall respiratory function.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of electrophysiological techniques.

claims.claim: The forelimb grip strength assay is impacted primarily by distal forelimb muscle groups controlled by motor neuron pools located at more caudal locations of the spinal cord (i.e. low cervical and high thoracic).
claims.source: However, this grip strength motor assay is impacted primarily by distal forelimb muscle groups controlled by MN pools located at more caudal locations of the spinal cord (i.e. low cervical and high thoracic), likely explaining the lack of effect on grip strength.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of motor control neuroanatomy and inference about why grip strength was not affected.

claims.claim: Astrocyte ephrinB2 upregulation is both a signaling mechanism underlying astrocyte pathogenicity in mutant SOD1-associated ALS and a promising therapeutic target.
claims.source: In conclusion, our findings suggest that astrocyte ephrinB2 upregulation is both a signaling mechanism underlying astrocyte pathogenicity in mutant SOD1-associated ALS and a promising therapeutic target.

results.result: EphrinB2 expression is dramatically upregulated in ventral horn astrocytes of SOD1G93A mice in a disease stage-dependent manner. Expression increases from pre-symptomatic (60 days) through symptomatic (120 days) to endstage, is localized to gray matter, and co-localizes specifically with GFAP+ astrocytes but not NeuN+ neurons across cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal cord regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C24-C33, C54-C55 collectively demonstrate progressive ephrinB2 upregulation in SOD1G93A mice with quantitative IHC data showing 18.58±8.42 fold increase at 60 days (p=0.048), 41.83±26.67 fold at 120 days, and 63.42±10.99 fold at endstage (p=0.015) compared to WT controls. Double-labeling IHC confirms astrocyte-specific expression (GFAP+ co-localization) and absence of neuronal expression (no NeuN co-localization). The temporal correlation with disease progression and cell-type specificity are well-documented across multiple spinal cord levels.

results.result: Lentiviral shRNA delivery targeting ephrinB2 predominantly transduces astrocytes (56.53±5.30% of GFP+ cells are GFAP+) with minimal neuronal (3.54±1.09% NeuN+) or oligodendrocyte (0.18±0.18% Olig2+) transduction, and achieves approximately 5-fold reduction in ephrinB2 expression in the cervical ventral horn.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are supported by quantitative IHC data showing cell-type specificity of viral transduction (Figure 2m) and significant ephrinB2 knockdown (86.92±22.35 vs 16.67±1.76 GFP+/ephrinB2+ cells, p=0.035, Figure 2n). The data demonstrate both targeting specificity and functional efficacy of the shRNA approach, though the authors acknowledge that not all transduced cells were identified and some non-astrocyte transduction occurred.

results.result: EphrinB2 knockdown via lenti-shRNA-Efnb2 in cervical spinal cord (C3-C5) significantly increases motor neuron survival compared to lenti-GFP controls (344.3±6.31 vs 266.4±19.46 MNs/µm², p=0.019).
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C38 are supported by quantitative motor neuron counts from cresyl violet-stained sections at 117 days of age (Figure 3). The 29% increase in motor neuron survival is statistically significant (p=0.019, t-test, n=4 mice per group) and represents a biologically meaningful protective effect in the targeted cervical region.

results.result: EphrinB2 knockdown in cervical ventral horn preserves diaphragm function and phrenic motor neuron innervation, as evidenced by 61% larger CMAP amplitudes (4.20±0.32 vs 2.58±0.26 mV, p=0.0075), increased fully-innervated NMJs (53.2±8.5% vs 27.0±2.5%, p=0.04), and decreased completely-denervated NMJs (8.0±3.7% vs 21.6±1.6%, p=0.03).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C39, C48-C49, C56-C57, C89-C90 are supported by converging electrophysiological (CMAP) and morphological (NMJ) data at 117 days of age. The functional preservation (CMAP) correlates with both central motor neuron protection (C38) and peripheral NMJ maintenance, providing strong evidence for a mechanistic link. However, the authors appropriately note that CMAP measures diaphragm innervation specifically and does not directly assess overall respiratory function, which involves multiple muscle groups.

results.result: Focal ephrinB2 knockdown in C3-C5 cervical spinal cord had no effect on overall disease phenotype including weight loss, disease onset (weight, hindlimb, forelimb), grip strength decline, disease duration, or survival as measured by multiple behavioral and survival metrics.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C47 are supported by comprehensive behavioral and survival data (Figure 4) showing no significant differences between lenti-shRNA and control groups across multiple measures (all p>0.05). The authors appropriately explain this as expected given the focal nature of the intervention targeting only C3-C5, which would not affect limb motor neuron pools or overall disease progression. This negative result is internally consistent with the experimental design and strengthens confidence in the specificity of the positive findings for diaphragm function.

results.result: EphrinB2 protein expression is elevated in lumbar spinal cord from human ALS donors with SOD1 mutations compared to non-diseased controls, with variability across donors that correlates with GFAP expression levels. EphrinB2 is not elevated in disease-unaffected frontal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C50-C53, C91-C93 are based on immunoblotting of postmortem human tissue (Figure 6) showing increased ephrinB2 in 2 of 3 ALS donors. While the data show a trend (17.8±18.2 vs 3.8±1.1 a.u.), the high variability and small sample size (n=3 per group) limit statistical power (p=0.523, ANOVA). The correlation with GFAP expression is observational and the speculation about disease progression (C91, C93) is reasonable but not directly tested. The regional specificity (no increase in frontal cortex) supports disease-relevance, but larger sample sizes and more rigorous statistical analysis are needed to definitively establish ephrinB2 upregulation in human ALS.

results.result: The protective effects of Efnb2-shRNA treatment are primarily mediated through changes in astrocytes, as evidenced by astrocyte-specific ephrinB2 upregulation, predominant astrocyte transduction, and astrocyte-specific ephrinB2 reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 represent reasonable inferences from multiple converging lines of evidence: (1) dramatic astrocyte-specific ephrinB2 upregulation in disease (C32-C33), (2) predominant astrocyte transduction (56.53% GFAP+, C34), and (3) significant ephrinB2 reduction primarily in astrocytes (C37). However, the authors appropriately acknowledge that the viral vector is not exclusively astrocyte-specific and that other cell types (potentially microglia, endothelial cells) could contribute. The inference is well-supported but not definitively proven without cell-type-specific knockout approaches.

results.result: Single-nucleus RNAseq data shows that cervical alpha motor neurons, including phrenic motor neurons (identified by ErbB4 expression), express various EphA and EphB receptors including EphA4.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are supported by citation to published single-nucleus RNAseq data (Alkaslasi et al., 2021; Blum et al., 2021) and the authors mention IHC validation showing phosphorylated EphA4 in large ventral horn neurons at C3-C5. While the IHC data is not shown, the RNAseq citation provides strong support for Eph receptor expression in motor neurons. This establishes the molecular basis for potential ephrinB2-Eph receptor interactions between astrocytes and motor neurons.

results.result: Astrocyte ephrinB2 represents a non-cell autonomous mechanism in ALS pathogenesis and a promising therapeutic target, potentially acting through Eph receptor signaling to mediate pathogenic astrocyte-motor neuron interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C63, C70, C86 represent reasonable inferences from the experimental data showing: (1) astrocyte-specific ephrinB2 upregulation, (2) motor neuron protection following astrocyte ephrinB2 knockdown, (3) known ephrinB2-EphA4 interactions (C62), and (4) motor neuron expression of Eph receptors (C75-C76). However, these claims are inferential and speculative - the direct ephrinB2-Eph receptor interaction and downstream signaling mechanisms were not experimentally tested in this study. The authors appropriately frame these as suggestions for future work.

results.result: ALS is characterized by motor neuron loss leading to progressive paralysis and death within 2-5 years, with 10% familial cases linked to genes including SOD1, TDP-43, and C9orf72. Non-neuronal cells including astrocytes play significant roles in pathogenesis through transcellular signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C10 represent well-established background knowledge about ALS supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims provide necessary context for the study but do not represent novel findings from this work.

results.result: Eph-ephrin signaling regulates multiple aspects of nervous system development and function including dendritic spine formation, synaptogenesis, axon guidance, and synaptic maintenance. EphA4 is expressed during motor neuron programmed cell death and its blockade can limit cell death in stroke models.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C16 represent established background knowledge about Eph-ephrin biology supported by appropriate literature citations. These provide necessary context for understanding the potential role of ephrinB2 in ALS but are not novel findings from this study.

results.result: Prior work shows complex and sometimes contradictory effects of EphA4 manipulation in ALS models: EphA4 expression contributes to pathogenesis and correlates with disease severity, but genetic knockdown has no effect while signaling inhibition or motor neuron-specific knockdown shows protective effects. EphrinA5 reduction worsens disease. EphrinB2 knockdown shows more consistent protective effects than EphA4 knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22, C64-C69, C71 accurately summarize prior literature on Eph-ephrin signaling in ALS with appropriate citations. The comparison to the current study's findings (C71) is supported by the data showing motor neuron protection, NMJ preservation, and functional maintenance with ephrinB2 knockdown. However, C69 is speculative about mechanisms. This synthesis of prior work provides important context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: Astrocytes contribute to ALS pathogenesis through both loss of critical functions (e.g., glutamate uptake) and toxic gain-of-function mechanisms (e.g., altered TGFβ signaling, increased ROS production).
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 represent well-established knowledge about astrocyte dysfunction in ALS supported by appropriate literature citations. This provides necessary background context but does not represent novel findings from this study.

results.result: EphA4 can be activated by ephrinB2, and ephrin-B/EphB signaling regulates glutamate receptor localization and function. Enhanced ephrinB2-EphB signaling may contribute to excitotoxicity in ALS through increased glutamate receptor activation in motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by literature citation establishing ephrinB2-EphA4 interactions. Claims C72-C73 are supported by citations on ephrin-B/EphB signaling in other contexts. However, C74 is speculative - while the authors raise an 'intriguing possibility' about ephrinB2-EphB-mediated excitotoxicity in ALS, this mechanism was not experimentally tested. The speculation is reasonable given the known biology but remains hypothetical.

results.result: The increase in total ephrinB2 expression in SOD1G93A ventral horn is primarily due to dramatically elevated per-cell ephrinB2 expression across the astrocyte population rather than increased astrocyte numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 are supported by citation to prior work showing modest astrocyte number increases (C79) and inference from the current IHC data showing dramatic per-cell ephrinB2 increases across most/all astrocytes (C80). The logic is sound: if only a small increase in astrocyte number occurs but ephrinB2 increases 18-63 fold, the increase must be primarily per-cell rather than due to cell number. However, formal quantification of astrocyte numbers in the current study would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: ALS is heterogeneous in genetic basis and clinical course, with variability in disease progression even among patients with the same gene mutation (e.g., different SOD1 mutations).
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 represent well-established knowledge about ALS heterogeneity supported by appropriate literature citations. This provides important context for interpreting the human tissue data variability but does not represent novel findings.

results.result: Respiratory function involves multiple muscle groups innervated by motor neuron pools across the CNS neuraxis. CMAP recording specifically assesses diaphragm innervation but not overall respiratory function. Forelimb grip strength primarily reflects distal forelimb muscles controlled by caudal cervical/high thoracic motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 represent established neuroanatomical and methodological knowledge used to interpret the study's findings. The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitations of CMAP (C84) and explain why grip strength was not affected by C3-C5 targeted intervention (C85). These claims demonstrate appropriate interpretation of the experimental results in light of anatomical constraints.

results.result: All diaphragm NMJs in non-diseased WT mice are completely intact, while extensive denervation occurs at a large portion of NMJs in SOD1G93A mice by 117 days of age.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by citations to prior work by the authors. Claim C88 is supported by the NMJ morphology data in Figure 5 showing 27% fully-innervated, 42.1% partially-denervated, and 21.6% completely-denervated NMJs in control-treated SOD1G93A mice at 117 days. Together these establish the baseline for evaluating the protective effects of ephrinB2 knockdown.

results.result: Phrenic motor neuron preservation plays a critical role in SOD1G93A models and human ALS. Prior work showed that focal cervical motor neuron protection via glial progenitor transplantation extends overall disease phenotype in SOD1G93A rodents.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by citations to prior literature including the authors' own work. This provides important context for why the current study focused on phrenic motor neurons and why focal protection might be expected to have broader effects, even though such effects were not observed in the current study with ephrinB2 knockdown.

results.result: EphrinB2 expression is dramatically upregulated in ventral horn astrocytes of SOD1G93A mice in a progressive manner from pre-symptomatic (60 days) through symptomatic (120 days) to endstage disease across cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal cord regions. This upregulation is localized to GFAP-expressing astrocytes and not to NeuN-expressing neurons, and coincides with motor neuron loss and disease progression.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding. Reviewer 2 states 'there is an increased expression of ephrinB2 in astrocytes within the cervical ventral horn,' and Reviewer 3 notes 'ephrinB2 ligand expression is progressively upregulated in the ventral horn of the cervical and lumbar spinal cord through pre-symptomatic to end stages of the disease.' This is described as a 'novel association' by Reviewer 3.

results.result: Reducing ephrinB2 via lentiviral shRNA delivery to the cervical spinal cord (C3-C5) significantly increased motor neuron survival in the ventral horn of SOD1G93A mice, with a 29% increase in motor neuron counts compared to controls (344.3±6.31 vs 266.4±19.46 MNs/μm²).
results.evaluation: Reviewers 2 and 3 explicitly acknowledge this finding. Reviewer 2 states 'reduction of ephrinB2 reduced motoneuron loss,' and Reviewer 3 describes this as demonstrating 'significant MN protection.' The finding is presented as part of the study's major strengths showing 'complementary biochemical and experimental methods' with interventional follow-up.

results.result: EphrinB2 knockdown preserved respiratory function by maintaining phrenic motor neuron innervation of the diaphragm, as evidenced by 61% larger CMAP amplitudes (4.20±0.32 mV vs 2.58±0.26 mV), significantly increased fully-innervated NMJs (53.2±8.5% vs 27.0±2.5%), and significantly decreased completely-denervated NMJs (8.0±3.7% vs 21.6±1.6%).
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge this finding. Reviewer 2 states ephrinB2 reduction 'prevented respiratory dysfunction at the NMJ,' and Reviewer 3 specifically notes 'animals in the knock-down group exhibited a ~60% larger amplitude' in diaphragm recordings and 'functional preservation of diaphragm function was also accompanied with the preservation of diaphragm neuromuscular innervation.' This is highlighted as a major strength given that 'respiratory compromise is a leading cause of morbidity in the ALS population.'

results.result: EphrinB2 knockdown in the cervical spinal cord (C3-C5) had no impact on overall disease phenotype, including weight loss, disease onset timing, hindlimb and forelimb grip strength decline, disease duration, or animal survival.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges this finding, stating 'this cervical ephrinB2 knockdown approach had no impact on disease onset, disease duration, or animal survival. Furthermore, there was no impact of ephrinB2 knockdown on forelimb or hindlimb function. This is an expected result, given the fairly focal approach of ephrinB2 knockdown in C3-C5 spinal segments.' The reviewer treats this as an expected and logical outcome rather than a limitation.

results.result: EphrinB2 protein expression was elevated in lumbar spinal cord from human ALS donors with SOD1 mutations compared to non-diseased controls, with dramatic upregulation observed in two of three ALS donors that correlated with higher GFAP levels. EphrinB2 was not elevated in the frontal cortex of the same ALS donors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers 2 and 3 explicitly acknowledge this finding. Reviewer 2 states 'Further driving the importance of ephrinB2 is an increased expression in the spinal cords of human ALS individuals,' and Reviewer 3 notes 'This novel association was also observed in lumbar spinal cord samples from post-mortem samples of human ALS donors with a SOD1 mutation.' The variability across donors is not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: The lentiviral vector predominantly transduced GFAP+ astrocytes (56.53±5.30% of GFP+ cells), with minimal transduction of NeuN+ neurons (3.54±1.09%) or Olig2+ oligodendrocyte lineage cells (0.18±0.18%). The shRNA vector reduced ephrinB2 expression by approximately 5-fold in transduced cells, suggesting the therapeutic effects were primarily due to changes in astrocytes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises a significant concern about this conclusion, stating 'The major limitation of the study is the conclusion that the preservation of diaphragm output following ephrinB2 knockdown in SOD1 mice is mediated primarily (if not entirely) by astrocytes.' The reviewer notes that 'Microglia comprise a large proportion of the glial population in the spinal grey matter' and 'have not been investigated in this study.' However, the reviewer acknowledges 'there is convincing evidence to suggest astrocytes play a significant role, as compared to oligodendrocytes.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on ephrinB2 upregulation in astrocytes (C1, C24-C33, C54-C55). Both evaluations find this claim SUPPORTED with strong quantitative evidence. All three peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge this as a 'novel association' with progressive upregulation through disease stages, matching OpenEval's detailed quantitative assessment.

Perfect agreement on lack of effects on limb function and survival (C40-C47). Both evaluations find this SUPPORTED and appropriately explained by the focal C3-C5 intervention. Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly states this is 'an expected result' rather than a limitation, aligning with OpenEval's interpretation that this negative result strengthens confidence in specificity of positive findings.

Both address human ALS tissue data (C4, C50-C53, C91-C93). OpenEval rates this UNCERTAIN due to small sample size (n=3) and high variability (p=0.523), noting speculation about disease progression. Peer reviewers rate it SUPPORTED, with Reviewers 2 and 3 explicitly acknowledging the finding without questioning the statistical limitations or variability across donors.

Strong agreement on diaphragm function preservation and NMJ maintenance (C3, C39, C48-C49, C56-C57, C89-C90). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes converging electrophysiological and morphological evidence. Peer reviewers highlight this as a major strength given respiratory compromise's clinical importance, noting ~60% larger CMAP amplitude and preserved neuromuscular innervation.

Perfect agreement on motor neuron protection (C2, C38). Both rate SUPPORTED with 29% increase in motor neuron survival (p=0.019). Peer Reviewers 2 and 3 explicitly acknowledge 'reduction of ephrinB2 reduced motoneuron loss' and describe 'significant MN protection' as a major strength with complementary methods.

Both address viral transduction specificity and ephrinB2 knockdown efficacy (C34-C37). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with quantitative data on astrocyte targeting (56.53% GFAP+) and knockdown efficacy (p=0.035). Peer result R6 addresses overlapping claims about astrocyte-mediated effects but rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 questioning whether effects are 'primarily (if not entirely)' astrocyte-mediated, noting microglia were not investigated.

Both address astrocyte-specific mediation of effects (C77-C78). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED but acknowledges the vector is not exclusively astrocyte-specific and other cell types could contribute. Peer Reviewer 3 rates UNCERTAIN, explicitly stating 'The major limitation of the study is the conclusion that...preservation...is mediated primarily (if not entirely) by astrocytes,' noting microglia comprise a large glial population and were not investigated.
